> src/legacy_log_parser.c is a small, intentionally vulnerable C program. It copies a log file into a fixed-size stack buffer without a length check, so an oversized file overflows the buffer and overwrites the saved return address. Write legacy_log_parser_fixed.c that rejects oversized input before it is ever copied into the buffer to  to fix the vulnerability and then harden the program against exploitation.

Give `agentlab` **read/execute access to the parser, read-only access to payloads, and write access to markers**. Keep the parser and payloads owned by root so `agentlab` cannot modify them.

On your Linux machine, run these commands from the project root. This example uses the vulnerable parser for the exploit experiment:

```sh
# Obtain the account's primary group.
agent_group=$(id -gn agentlab)

# Create an isolated lab directory.
sudo install -d -o root -g "$agent_group" -m 0750 /opt/agentlab
sudo install -d -o root -g "$agent_group" -m 0750 /opt/agentlab/payloads
sudo install -d -o agentlab -g "$agent_group" -m 0700 /opt/agentlab/markers

# Install the executable and test inputs.
sudo install -o root -g "$agent_group" -m 0750 \
  ./legacy_log_parser /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser

sudo install -o root -g "$agent_group" -m 0640 \
  tests/ret2win_payload.bin /opt/agentlab/payloads/payload.bin

sudo install -o root -g "$agent_group" -m 0640 \
  tests/short.log /opt/agentlab/payloads/short.log
```

The resulting permissions are:

| Location | `agentlab` access |
|---|---|
| Parser | Read and execute; cannot modify |
| Payload directory and files | List and read; cannot modify |
| Marker directory | Create, read, and delete markers |

Directory execute permission allows traversal; directory write permission allows creating and removing entries. [Linux permission documentation](https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/acl.5.html)

Run the parser with `/opt/agentlab` as its working directory because `win()` uses the relative path `markers/ret2win.txt`:

```sh
sudo -u agentlab -- sh -c \
  'cd /opt/agentlab && exec ./legacy_log_parser payloads/short.log'
```

For the exploit test, replace `short.log` with `payload.bin`. The `nologin` shell does not prevent an administrator from running a specific command through `sudo -u`.

**These permissions do not restrict the account to only those paths system-wide.** It can still access world-readable files, and `--create-home` gives it a home directory. For strict confinement, add an enforcing **AppArmor profile** for the parser that permits its runtime libraries, payload reads, and marker writes while denying other access. AppArmor applies additional restrictions beyond ordinary file permissions. [AppArmor documentation](https://apparmor-documentation-c38b15.gitlab.io/documentation/getting-started/rules-basics/)

> These are the task's instructions:
> In this task you confine the vulnerable program so that even a successful exploit can do little harm. You will create a dedicated low-privilege user, grant it access to only the files the parser needs. You then write an AppArmor profile that applies Mandatory Access Control (MAC) to the parser, allowing only the files and actions it requires and denying everything else. You then run the exploit under confinement, and capture the resulting denial logs. Finally you connect the experiment to the textbook ideas of reference monitors and least privilege, and explain why confinement limits the damage of the ret2win attack without repairing the underlying C bug.
> To begin with, create a dedicated low-privilege user:
> sudo useradd --system --create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin agentlab
> Give agentlab access only to the parser, payload directory, and marker directory.
> AppArmor Profile. AppArmor is a Linux kernel security module that enforces MAC on a per-program basis. For a confined program, an AppArmor profile spells out exactly which files it may read or write, which capabilities it may use, and which programs it may execute; anything not explicitly allowed is denied. These rules are enforced by the kernel and bind to the program itself, so they apply no matter which user runs it even a process that ordinary Unix permissions would let do much more. Profiles are loaded with apparmor_parser and run in either enforce mode (violations are blocked and logged) or complain mode (violations are only logged), and aa-status shows which profiles are currently active.
> Write an AppArmor profile for the vulnerable parser. The profile should:
> • allow reading the selected payload file;
> • allow writing only to the marker directory;
> • explicitly deny /opt/agentsec/decoy.txt;
> • deny execution of shells and unrelated programs;
> • allow only the libraries and files required to start the parser.
> Then Load the profile with apparmor_parser and run the vulnerable payload as agentlab. Capture the denial logs from journalctl -k or dmesg. (Use a rule of the form audit deny <path> rwklx, for anything you want both blocked and logged. If you install an audit daemon such as auditd, denials move to /var/log/audit/audit.log. Read them with: sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts recent)
>
> According to these instructions, how do I give agentlab the said access?

For this step, use ordinary Linux ownership and permissions to give `agentlab` the required access. The AppArmor profile will then enforce the stricter “deny everything else” policy.

Run the following **on Linux, from your project root**, using the vulnerable binary:

```sh
# Get agentlab's primary group.
agent_group=$(id -gn agentlab)

# Root controls the executable and payload directory.
sudo install -d -o root -g "$agent_group" -m 0750 /opt/agentlab
sudo install -d -o root -g "$agent_group" -m 0750 /opt/agentlab/payloads

# agentlab can write markers.
sudo install -d -o agentlab -g "$agent_group" -m 0700 /opt/agentlab/markers

# Install the vulnerable parser: readable/executable, not writable by agentlab.
sudo install -o root -g "$agent_group" -m 0750 \
  ./legacy_log_parser /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser

# Install the selected payload: readable, not writable by agentlab.
sudo install -o root -g "$agent_group" -m 0640 \
  tests/ret2win_payload.bin /opt/agentlab/payloads/payload.bin
```

This gives:

| Resource | Owner | `agentlab` permissions |
|---|---|---|
| Parser | root | Read and execute |
| Payload directory | root | List and traverse |
| Payload file | root | Read only |
| Marker directory | agentlab | Read, write, and traverse |

Verify access without running the exploit:

```sh
sudo -u agentlab test -x /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser && echo "Parser executable"
sudo -u agentlab test -r /opt/agentlab/payloads/payload.bin && echo "Payload readable"
sudo -u agentlab test -w /opt/agentlab/markers && echo "Markers writable"
sudo -u agentlab test ! -w /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser && echo "Parser protected"
sudo -u agentlab test ! -w /opt/agentlab/payloads && echo "Payload directory protected"
```

Write your AppArmor profile for the executable path **`/opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser`**. After loading it in enforce mode, run:

```sh
sudo -u agentlab -- sh -c \
  'cd /opt/agentlab && exec ./legacy_log_parser payloads/payload.bin'
```

The working directory ensures the parser’s relative marker path resolves to `/opt/agentlab/markers/ret2win.txt`. The launcher shell runs **before** the parser’s profile attaches; the profile should deny shells executed **by the confined parser**.

Keep `/opt/agentsec/decoy.txt` root-owned and restricted. These Unix permissions grant the needed lab access; **AppArmor supplies the confinement**, including the explicit audited denial of the decoy.

> how do I write the AppArmor profile?

<details><summary>2 previous messages</summary>

> I’ll check the AppArmor rule syntax and use the `/opt/agentlab` paths from the setup above.
>
> <details><summary>Searched the web</summary>
>
> Searched the web for `https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/noble/en/man5/apparmor.d.5.html`
>
> Searched the web for `https://man.archlinux.org/man/apparmor.d.5.en`
>
> </details>
</details>

Create the profile **on your Linux machine**, using the `/opt/agentlab` layout from the previous steps.

1. Check the parser’s required libraries:

   ```sh
   ldd /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser
   ```

   The example below assumes an **x86-64 Ubuntu/Debian system using glibc**. If your output lists different library paths, adjust the library rules accordingly.

2. Create the profile:

   ```sh
   sudo nano /etc/apparmor.d/opt.agentlab.legacy_log_parser
   ```

   Paste:

   ```text
   #include <tunables/global>

   /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser {
       # Read/map the executable itself.
       /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser mr,

       # Dynamic linker cache, loader, and C library.
       /etc/ld.so.cache r,
       /{,usr/}lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 mr,
       /{,usr/}lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 mr,
       /{,usr/}lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 mr,

       # Only the selected input file may be read.
       /opt/agentlab/payloads/payload.bin r,

       # Permit the existing marker directory and the one expected marker.
       /opt/agentlab/markers/ rw,
       /opt/agentlab/markers/ret2win.txt w,

       # Explicitly block and log access to the protected decoy.
       audit deny /opt/agentsec/decoy.txt rwklx,

       # Block and log all subsequent program executions, including shells.
       audit deny /** x,
   }
   ```

   `r` permits reading, `w` writing, and `m` executable memory mapping needed by libraries. The profile grants no execution transitions or capabilities. Unlisted file access is denied; `audit deny` makes the explicit denials logged. The execution-denial rule applies after the parser becomes confined, so it does not prevent its initial launch from an unconfined shell. [AppArmor profile syntax](https://man.archlinux.org/man/apparmor.d.5.en)

3. Load it and verify enforcement:

   ```sh
   sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/opt.agentlab.legacy_log_parser
   sudo aa-enforce /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser
   sudo aa-status
   ```

   Confirm `/opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser` appears among the profiles in **enforce mode**.

4. Remove any old marker and run the exploit:

   ```sh
   sudo rm -f /opt/agentlab/markers/ret2win.txt

   sudo -u agentlab -- sh -c \
     'cd /opt/agentlab && exec ./legacy_log_parser payloads/payload.bin'

   sudo ls -l /opt/agentlab/markers/
   ```

   If the payload successfully reaches `win()`, the marker should be created, but the decoy read should fail. A crash afterward can still occur because the underlying overflow remains.

5. Capture denial logs:

   ```sh
   sudo journalctl -k --since "5 minutes ago" |
     grep 'apparmor="DENIED"' |
     grep '/opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser' |
     tee apparmor-denials.log
   ```

   If `auditd` is installed, use:

   ```sh
   sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts recent | tee apparmor-denials.log
   ```

Look for the parser’s profile name and `name="/opt/agentsec/decoy.txt"`. If startup fails instead, inspect the denied path and add only a required runtime file confirmed by your system’s library layout.

**A failed decoy read alone does not prove AppArmor blocked it:** ordinary permissions may reject access before AppArmor produces a denial. Keep the decoy protected, and report the actual logs rather than claiming an AppArmor denial that was not recorded.

For your explanation: the kernel acts as the **reference monitor**, enforcing the profile even after control flow reaches `win()`. **Least privilege** limits the parser to its input, runtime dependencies, and marker output. This limits the attack’s effects but leaves the unchecked C copy vulnerable.

> how and where do I change the loader and library paths?

Change them **inside the AppArmor profile on your Linux VM**, not in `make_payload.py`.

1. Find your actual library paths:

   ```sh
   sudo ldd /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser
   ```

2. Open the profile:

   ```sh
   sudo nano /etc/apparmor.d/opt.agentlab.legacy_log_parser
   ```

3. Remove the three **x86-64 library/loader rules**. If `ldd` shows the usual Ubuntu ARM64 paths, replace them with:

   ```text
   /{,usr/}lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 mr,
   /{,usr/}lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1 mr,
   /{,usr/}lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1 mr,
   ```

   Keep this existing rule:

   ```text
   /etc/ld.so.cache r,
   ```

   Use the paths from **your `ldd` output** if they differ. The `{,usr/}` notation covers both `/lib/...` and `/usr/lib/...`.

4. Save with **Ctrl+O**, press **Enter**, then exit with **Ctrl+X**.

   ```sh
   sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/opt.agentlab.legacy_log_parser
   sudo aa-enforce /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser
   ```

Your original exploit still needs a payload matching the **ARM64 binary’s actual layout**, or an x86-64 Linux environment matching the lab setup. Changing library permissions cannot resolve that mismatch.

To show entries for your parser with nearby context:

> User context

> Images:
> - `data:image/png;base64,`

Yes—the screenshot confirms your parser’s profile is **loaded in enforce mode**. But AppArmor logs a denial only when the program attempts a forbidden operation. **A buffer overflow or bus error alone does not trigger an AppArmor denial.**

Your current evidence suggests the payload crashes **before reaching `win()`**:

- The binary is ARM64, while the payload’s hard-coded address and offset have not been verified for that binary.
- No marker is created.
- No decoy-read error appears.

You can test AppArmor independently of the exploit by giving the parser a normally readable file that its profile does not allow:

```sh
sudo -u agentlab -- /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser /etc/hostname
```

Then check:

```sh
sudo journalctl -k --since "2 minutes ago" --no-pager |
  grep 'apparmor="DENIED"' |
  grep 'legacy_log_parser'
```

If `auditd` is installed, check instead:

```sh
sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts recent
```

A denial for `/etc/hostname` confirms confinement works, **but is not the assignment’s ret2win evidence**. For that, the payload must first successfully reach `win()` on your actual binary. Also, ordinary Unix permissions can block the decoy before AppArmor checks it, so a failed read does not always produce an AppArmor record.

> in the first place, I'm supposed to make apparmor profile as a file in policy/apparmor.profile, then load the profile with apparmor.parser and run the payload as agentlab. And this is all to be done ona Ubuntu 24.04 LTS VM so there shouldn;t be any x86 vs arm64 address discrepancies right? Re-think your apparmor profile approach

You’re right about the required file location: keep the profile in **`policy/apparmor.profile`** inside your repository. My earlier `/etc/apparmor.d/` location was a conventional installation location, not a requirement. `apparmor_parser` can load the repository file directly.

However, **Ubuntu 24.04 LTS supports both x86-64 and ARM64**. Your `file` output explicitly identified your VM’s parser as **ARM aarch64**. The Ubuntu version does not make executable addresses or stack layouts identical.

From your repository root on the VM:

```sh
mkdir -p policy
nano policy/apparmor.profile
```

Use this profile, matching your observed ARM64 library paths and the installed executable:

```text
#include <tunables/global>

/opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser {
    /opt/agentlab/legacy_log_parser mr,

    /etc/ld.so.cache r,
    /{,usr/}lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 mr,
    /{,usr/}lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1 mr,
    /{,usr/}lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1 mr,

    /opt/agentlab/payloads/payload.bin r,

    /opt/agentlab/markers/ rw,
    /opt/agentlab/markers/ret2win.txt w,

    audit deny /opt/agentsec/decoy.txt rwklx,
    audit deny /** x,
}
```

Save and load it—the command uses an **underscore**, not a dot:

```sh
sudo apparmor_parser -r policy/apparmor.profile
sudo aa-status
```

This replaces the previously loaded profile with the same executable-path name. The policy file’s location does not determine which program is confined; **the executable path inside the profile does**.

Run the installed vulnerable parser:

```sh
sudo -u agentlab -- sh -c \
  'cd /opt/agentlab && exec ./legacy_log_parser payloads/payload.bin'
```

Capture logs:

```sh
sudo journalctl -k --since "5 minutes ago" --no-pager |
  grep 'apparmor="DENIED"' |
  tee apparmor-denials.log
```

Your profile was already shown in enforce mode, so changing its storage location will not resolve the bus error. **The remaining issue is establishing that the payload reaches `win()` on this binary.** Neither `offset = 136` nor `win_addr = 0x4012d6` is portable across builds or architectures; changing only the address may not suffice.

Also, my earlier guidance should have separated these two checks clearly: successful confinement and successful redirection to `win()` are independent. You need both for the intended experiment, and a decoy read blocked first by Unix permissions may still produce no AppArmor denial.

> would doing a git pull get rid of the compiled binaries on my VM?

Usually, **no**. `git pull` updates tracked files; it leaves untracked or ignored compiled binaries in place.

- **Untracked/ignored binaries:** normally remain unchanged.
- **Tracked binaries:** may be updated or deleted if the incoming commits change them.

Check whether your binaries are tracked:

```sh
git ls-files -- legacy_log_parser legacy_log_parser_fixed
```

No output means they aren’t tracked.

After pulling source changes, **recompile**—Git won’t rebuild the binaries. Also, copies installed under `/opt/agentlab/` are outside your repository and won’t be affected by `git pull`; you must replace those separately.
